solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Plant's men rebuked in the past

parts.note: OR = other ranks, the ordinary soldiers
chid is the old past tense of chide

explanation.surface: A gardener's staff were told off long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant's' reads as a factory's workforce; the 's is just 'is' joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the orchid is one family among flowering plants.

clue.text: Authorised agents left behind inoperative insurgents at first

indicators.note: to be behind is to come after

parts.note: a machine that is off is not operating

indicators.note: what comes at first in a word is its opening letter, here the I of insurgents

parts.note: first letter of insurgents
the American intelligence agency
L = left

explanation.surface: Licensed spies leave rebels behind, stranded and out of action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Authorised agents' looks like a single phrase, but only the first word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain adjective synonym: an official visit or result is one sanctioned by those in charge.

clue.text: One leaves revolutionary Russian leader after tea in bed

parts.note: cha is slang for tea

indicators.note: a revolution is a full turn, so a revolutionary word is turned round: LENN becomes NNEL
placed after means written later

parts.note: Lenin led the Russian revolution; drop the I and turn the rest round

explanation.surface: A revolutionary leader lies in bed while someone slips out after tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' seems to describe Lenin, which it fairly does, but its job is to turn LENN round. The definition is the last word: a river bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A less common sense of bed: the bed a river runs in is its channel.

clue.text: Understand trainee contracted by sandwich shop

indicators.note: by means beside, as in a house by the sea

parts.note: an intern is a trainee; cut off the N
Pret A Manger is a British sandwich chain

explanation.surface: A trainee has signed a contract with a sandwich shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contracted by' reads as employed by, but 'contracted' shortens the trainee and 'by' just places the shop alongside. Pret A Manger is a sandwich chain found all over Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: to interpret a remark is to take it, or understand it, in a certain way.

clue.text: The author's explosive books coming very soon

parts.note: the author = the setter = I; I'm = I am
a mine is an explosive device
NT = New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A writer announces an explosive new book is on its way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The author's' means the setter speaking: I'm. 'Explosive books' reads as sensational titles but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym phrased as a paraphrase: an imminent storm is one about to break.

clue.text: Emperor wrongly claims usurer steals gold

indicators.note: a thief keeps stolen goods inside his coat
letters put down wrongly are out of their proper order, so CLAIMS USURER is rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A ruler falsely accuses a moneylender of stealing gold.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a courtroom scene with the emperor as judge; in fact the emperor is the answer and the usurer merely supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from AD 161 to 180, the philosopher-emperor.

clue.text: Bar in New York for locals avoided by poor actor

parts.note: used as itself

indicators.note: if the ham avoids Gotham he stays out of it

parts.note: Gotham is a nickname for New York City
a ham is a bad, overacting actor; remove it

explanation.surface: A New York bar that regulars keep but a failing actor steers clear of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar in New York' suggests a drinking place; the bar is a gold bar and 'in' is a piece of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Bar in its metal sense: an ingot is a cast block of gold or other metal.

clue.text: Former temporary accommodation areas

parts.note: ex = former, as in ex-wife
tents are temporary shelters

explanation.surface: A notice listing old sites of temporary housing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former temporary accommodation' reads as a single phrase; only 'areas' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the extent of a forest is the area it covers.

clue.text: Hurled professor's chair

indicators.note: a professor is one who professes, declaring things out loud, so the professor's chair is the word as said

parts.note: a throne is a chair of state

explanation.surface: An academic's chair has been flung across the room.
explanation.walkthrough: A professor's 'chair' is their post, which seems the whole point; the setter uses 'professor's' to mean the word as declared. The signal is loose, so lean on the crossers.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a ball thrown is a ball hurled.

clue.text: Can clergyman definitely not put up bloke in flat?

indicators.note: in tells us the next pieces go inside the word for flat

parts.note: plain means flat, as flat country

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means the phrase is read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: 'No sir!' is an emphatic refusal
chap is a synonym for bloke

explanation.surface: Asking whether a clergyman can refuse to accommodate a man in his apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a modal verb opening a question, but it is slang for prison, so the definition is a jail's clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: A prison chaplain is a minister serving in a jail, and 'can' is slang for jail.

clue.text: Sycophant judge turned to grab near the end

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold
a word turned faces the other way

parts.note: a ref (referee) judges a match
the latter part is the part near the end

explanation.surface: A fawning judge changes sides to seize something as the case closes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like part of the definition, but the definition is only 'Sycophant'; the judge is a referee.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sycophant wins favour by flattering the powerful.

clue.text: Fish edging towards reptile in Everglades

parts.note: a gar is a long-snouted fish
to = towards

explanation.surface: A fish drifts nervously towards an alligator in a Florida swamp.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is one Florida scene, and the fish really is edging towards the reptile; 'edging' is doing the wrapping.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional word: gator is American shorthand for the alligators of the Florida swamps.

clue.text: Rumours about informer briefly meeting senior officer

indicators.note: things meeting come together end to end

parts.note: ca = circa, about
a nark is a police informer; lose the K
DS = detective sergeant

explanation.surface: Gossip spreads about a police informant meeting a senior detective.
explanation.walkthrough: The police surface keeps 'informer' and 'officer' looking like people in a story. A nark is British slang for a police informer.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowing from French: a canard (literally a duck) is a false or baseless rumour.

clue.text: So far ahead, pull on clogs

parts.note: a team two up is ahead

indicators.note: to clog a pipe is to block it from inside

parts.note: to tow is to pull
used as itself

explanation.surface: Well ahead so far, someone puts on wooden shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clogs' looks like footwear being pulled on; it is a verb, ON blocking up TOW.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom swapped for another: up to now and so far both mean until the present moment.

clue.text: More competent Republican on board? Not initially

indicators.note: in an across clue, the party letter is placed on, that is after, the shortened word
the word for board loses its opening letter

parts.note: a board is a table, as in 'bed and board'

explanation.surface: A question about whether bringing a Republican onto the company board would make it more capable.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks the clue in two: 'Not initially' acts on the board, not on the Republican.
explanation.definitionFit: Abler is the comparative of able, so more skilled or capable.

clue.text: Narrowly avoided collision — one arm is shaking, somewhat

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the phrase is taken

parts.note: oNE ARM IS Shaking

explanation.surface: After nearly crashing, a driver's arm is still trembling.
explanation.walkthrough: The trembling arm is exactly what a near miss leaves behind, which keeps the solver in the scene rather than reading the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the term comes from aviation and driving, where two vehicles nearly collide.

clue.text: I act macho, stirring coffee

indicators.note: stirring moves things around a cup, so the letters of I ACT MACHO are moved around

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A man swaggers while stirring his coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stirring' belongs so naturally with coffee that it hides its job of mixing the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a macchiato is one kind of coffee, espresso with a dash of milk.

clue.text: Artist sent Marx crazy

indicators.note: crazy means disordered in the head, so the letters of SENT MARX are thrown into disorder

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A painter drove Karl Marx mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Marx points to philosophy; the artist is a surrealist, which suits a clue about madness.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Max Ernst was a German Dada and surrealist painter.

clue.text: Prime minister, primarily Tory one who loathes cuddling children

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the first letter of Tory is used

parts.note: first letter of Tory

indicators.note: to cuddle is to hold in your arms

parts.note: a hater loathes
ch = children, as in census forms

explanation.surface: A Tory leader is accused of loathing children even while hugging them.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Thatcher was the Conservative (Tory) prime minister from 1979 to 1990, so the political surface points straight at her.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Margaret Thatcher held the office from 1979 to 1990.

clue.text: Husband rather against emptying out home, naturally

parts.note: a bit means rather, somewhat

indicators.note: emptying out a word removes its insides, leaving its first and last letters

parts.note: first and last letters of against

explanation.surface: A husband who is quite opposed to clearing out the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition's 'naturally' tells you it is a home in nature.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitat is the natural environment where an animal or plant lives.

clue.text: Accountant defending economic forecaster in emergency committee

indicators.note: defenders stand round what they guard

parts.note: CA = chartered accountant
the Office for Budget Responsibility, which forecasts the UK economy

explanation.surface: An accountant stands up for an economist before a crisis committee.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBR is the UK's official budget watchdog, which is why it counts as an economic forecaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A British proper name: COBRA, after Cabinet Office Briefing Room A, is where the government's crisis committee meets.

clue.text: Boozy sessions with outspoken groups of girls

indicators.note: outspoken literally means spoken out, so the word is what you hear rather than what you read

parts.note: a bevy is a group, especially of girls

explanation.surface: Frank-talking hen parties out on the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outspoken' seems to describe the girls, and the whole scene is a rowdy night out.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang: a bevvy is a drink, and also a drinking session.

clue.text: Extremely polite Disney princess raised like princess in fairytale

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising lifts the letters bottom to top, so PEELSA reads upwards
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so polite gives P and E

parts.note: the outer letters of PolitE
Elsa, heroine of Frozen

explanation.surface: A very courteous Disney heroine was brought up like a fairytale princess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for polite; it means the ends. The setter uses 'princess' twice on purpose: once in the wordplay, once in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion: Sleeping Beauty lay asleep for a hundred years.

clue.text: Reduce intoxication: live right, stopping liquid lunch?

indicators.note: stopping as in stopping a gap: the pieces plug the middle of the soup

parts.note: soup is a lunch you drink
to be is to live or exist

explanation.surface: Advice to a drinker: live properly and stop having boozy lunches to sober up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liquid lunch' reads as a boozy meal, but it is soup; BE and R go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To sober up is to recover from drinking, which lowers one's intoxication.

clue.text: Country's two rivers

definitions.note: Country's is used as an adjective, of the countryside

parts.note: R = river
the Ural is a river flowing from Russia into the Caspian Sea

explanation.surface: A nation is known for its two rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' suggests a nation, but it means the countryside. One river is the abbreviation R, the other a named river.
explanation.definitionFit: A possessive standing for an adjective: the country's ways are rural ways, as opposed to the town's.

clue.text: Briefly leave her fermenting port

indicators.note: fermenting liquid bubbles and churns, so the letters churn into a new order
'Briefly' cuts a letter off

parts.note: LEAVE is the word 'leave' itself
used as itself

explanation.surface: Leave her port wine to mature for a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' next to 'fermenting' reads as the fortified wine; it is a French harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Le Havre is a major French seaport at the mouth of the Seine.

clue.text: Key person agreeing to remove idiot

indicators.note: to remove is to take away

parts.note: one who assents agrees
an ass is an idiot; take it away

explanation.surface: A crucial yes-man agrees to get rid of a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key person' reads as a vital figure; the key is on a keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Enter is one of the keys on a computer keyboard.

clue.text: Notice you left case with no end of enthusiastic praise

parts.note: an ad is a notice advertising something
U is text-speak for you

indicators.note: with no means the following letter is removed from the word for case

parts.note: an action is a legal case

indicators.note: end of picks out the last letter of enthusiastic

explanation.surface: An ad tells you you've left a case without enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is the legal sense, a lawsuit, not a container; 'end of enthusiastic' names the one letter it loses.
explanation.definitionFit: Adulation is extravagant admiration, a stronger form of praise.

clue.text: Impatient panel tut vigorously

indicators.note: something shaken vigorously is thoroughly jumbled, so PANEL TUT is rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: An irritable committee tuts loudly in disapproval.
explanation.walkthrough: A tutting panel is exactly what petulance looks like, so the definition sits inside its own picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: petulant describes childish, irritable impatience.

clue.text: My inflexible garment

parts.note: cor! and my! are both exclamations of surprise
set in one's ways = inflexible

explanation.surface: Someone complains about their stiff piece of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks possessive but is the exclamation, as in 'My, that's tight!' Cor is British slang for the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a corset is a stiffened undergarment, and inflexible describes it well.
